meta.title: Someone Else Owns the Bass Note
meta.summary: Hold a triad on the top three strings with something lower sounding and you are not choosing the inversion — the bass is, leaving you only register and motion to decide.

— C major, second inversion, the fifth on the bottom. Now put a bass under it and read what the room actually hears.
Your grip never changed a note. Inversion is about the lowest
note, not the lowest note of whatever you happen to be holding — and on a top-set triad, with a band around you, that note is somebody else's.

. It specifies one lowest note, so it is written at whoever is going to play the lowest note — normally the bassist. Comping up here with a bass player in the room, you do not have to honour it at all; the chord above it is your job. Playing alone, nobody else is going to play it, so it is yours.
That leaves you exactly two decisions, and they are the two this chapter has been building:
— the register the chord sits in — and
— how little your hand has to move to get there. Not what the chord is called.
The register argument pays off here. A bass guitar's lowest string is tuned a full octave below the guitar's
, while strings 1-2-3 hold C major from

. A compact triad up there hands the whole low register to the bass and sits at or above the top of most sung melodies — nobody is standing on anybody. That is the standard way a rhythm section divides the range up, and it makes the three-string triad one of the most widely used textures in rhythm guitar: not the only one, but the default wherever a guitarist shares a rhythm section with a bass player.
